lead: VR, AR and MR answer one question: how much of the real world should the computer keep, and how much should it replace? VR replaces your view entirely. AR draws virtual content on top of the real view. MR lets a virtual object sit behind your real coffee table. The difference is not the headset or the brand. It is three tests you can state and measure: what reaches your eye, whether the system knows where the room is, and whether virtual content is anchored to and hidden by real things.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the four definitions and 1.5 for the components compared here.

sections.h3: Three tests, not a product list

blocks.text: A difference you can defend in an exam comes from a test, not a feeling. Products change every year; the tests do not.

Test 1 — how much of the real world reaches your eye. In VR the display is opaque: no light from the room reaches you, and the computer supplies every pixel. In AR the real world is the background and virtual content is drawn over it. MR is also see-through, but the system additionally reads the shape of the room.

Test 2 — does the system know where the real world is? VR needs only your own pose: where your head and hands are inside its own coordinate frame. The room is never drawn, so no map of it is needed. Modern headsets get that pose by SLAM or visual-inertial odometry, but they do not register content to real surfaces. AR and MR must register the virtual world to the real one, so a label sits on the right engine part and not 20 cm to its left. Registration uses markers, natural features or SLAM; the mechanics are in Unit 6.

Test 3 — is virtual content anchored to real objects and hidden by them? In simple AR a virtual arrow floats over everything, and the real table in front never covers it. In MR the arrow goes behind the real table when the table is nearer. That needs depth: the system must know the table is 0.6 m away and the arrow is 1.2 m away.
hidden if z_v > z_r ; draw if z_v ≤ z_r
blocks.where: z_v is the distance from your eye to the virtual surface, in metres; z_r is the distance from your eye to the nearest real surface along the same line of sight, in metres. The system writes real depths into the depth buffer first, then draws the virtual object; the usual depth test hides pixels that fail.

blocks.text: The definition used in this chapter. MR = AR plus per-pixel depth of the real scene. Anchoring to a plane or marker already exists in AR; MR adds metric depth, so virtual content is placed in 3D and correctly hidden by real objects. Some syllabi fold MR into AR; write your definition in the first line and stay consistent.

sections.h3: The same three tests on real hardware

blocks.text: The tests become a table. Read down a column for one technology; read across a row to see where two differ.

blocks.text: Phone AR sits at the low end of tests 2 and 3. The phone knows its own pose in the room but usually not that the real coffee table stands in front of your virtual sofa. A headset with depth sensors does. That is the practical line between AR and MR today.

sections.h3: Content, interaction, mobility, cost and safety

items: Content. VR is fully synthetic: every object is modelled. AR overlays a few virtual objects on a real view. MR merges both, and virtual objects respond to real surfaces — rest on the real floor, stop at the real wall.

Interaction. VR uses controllers, tracked hands and gaze. AR often needs free hands, so input is voice, gaze or a phone tap; a technician holds a spanner, not a controller. MR allows direct 3D manipulation of objects in the room.
Mobility. Phone AR is the most mobile, because it is the phone you already carry. VR headsets are tethered or limited by battery.
Cost. In the usual consumer range, phone AR is cheapest, a plain VR headset comes next, and a headset with real-scene depth for occlusion costs the most.
Safety. In VR you cannot see the room, so clear the floor before you start. In AR and MR the room is visible, but you can still walk into a door while watching the overlay.

blocks.text: Choose by the tests, not by fashion. Use VR when the real world would only get in the way: a surgical drill, a flight deck, a factory line not built yet. Use AR when the real world is the subject and the user needs free hands. Use MR when virtual objects must behave as physically present — fit, occlusion, layout.

examples.question: For each case choose VR, AR or MR and justify in one line. (a) A medical student practises a knee operation with no patient. (b) A technician servicing a tractor engine needs both hands free with the manual in view. (c) A shopper checks whether a 2.4 m sofa fits a 2.7 m wall, and wants the sofa to look right behind a coffee table 0.6 m in front of the sofa. Compute the clearance left on the wall.
steps: Test 1, is the real world needed? (a) No, the anatomy must replace the room, so VR. (b) Yes, the engine is the subject, so AR or MR. (c) Yes, the wall and floor are the subject, so AR or MR.

Test 2, must the system know where the real world is? (a) Only head and tool pose, which VR tracks already. (b) The overlay must sit on the correct engine part, so registration is needed, so AR. (c) The sofa must sit on the real floor against the real wall, so registration is needed, so AR or MR.

Test 3, must real objects hide virtual ones? (b) Nothing has to hide the overlay; free hands and a stable overlay are enough, so AR. (c) The sofa must disappear behind the coffee table at 0.6 m, so occlusion is needed, so MR.
Clearance on the wall: 2.7 m − 2.4 m = 0.3 m of total spare width.
If the sofa is centred, that spare width splits into 0.3 m ÷ 2 = 0.15 m on each side.
Answers: (a) VR, (b) AR, (c) MR — AR only if the shopper accepts a sofa that floats in front of the coffee table.
examples.answer: (a) VR, (b) AR, (c) MR; the sofa leaves 0.3 m of clearance on the wall, that is 0.15 m on each side when centred.
examples.check:
wall = 2.7
sofa = 2.4
gap = wall - sofa
print(round(gap, 2))
print(round(gap / 2, 2))

traps: "VR is more immersive" is not a difference. It names a feeling, not a test. Answer with the three tests.
AR and MR are not separated by the headset. A phone does AR; a headset with cameras can do either. Depth sensing and occlusion separate them.
Do not call a camera pass-through view on a VR headset "AR" by reflex. If it anchors content to the room and hides it behind real objects, it is MR here.
Fix your definition of MR in the first line. If you place MR inside AR, do not later describe it as standing between AR and VR.
Occlusion needs depth of the real scene. A marker gives pose, not depth; the marker alone cannot hide a virtual object.

quiz.q: State the three tests used to separate VR, AR and MR.
quiz.a: Test 1: how much of the real world reaches the eye. Test 2: whether the system knows where the real world is, that is, whether it registers virtual content to it. Test 3: whether virtual content is anchored to real objects and hidden by them.

quiz.q: Define MR as used in this chapter.
quiz.a: MR is AR plus per-pixel depth of the real scene, so virtual objects are anchored to real surfaces and can be occluded by real objects.

quiz.q: Why does VR not need to register content to the real room, while AR does?
quiz.a: VR draws every pixel itself, so it needs only the user's pose in its own coordinate frame. Modern headsets get that pose by SLAM or visual-inertial odometry, but no real-world map or registration is required. AR draws on a view of the real room, so it must know where the camera is relative to real surfaces.

quiz.q: Give one reason a phone AR app rarely hides a virtual object behind a real chair.
quiz.a: The phone usually has no depth map of the room, so it does not know the chair is nearer than the virtual object. Without z_r it cannot test z_v > z_r, so it simply draws the object on top.

quiz.q: A worker repairing a transformer must keep both hands on a wrench while reading the next step of a procedure. Which technology, and which test decides it?
quiz.a: AR. The real transformer is the subject (test 1 keeps the real view) and the hands must stay free, so the overlay is voice or gaze controlled. No real object has to hide the overlay, so test 3 does not force MR.

quiz.q: A furniture app must place a virtual sofa on the real floor and hide its lower edge behind a real sofa in front. Which test decides the technology, and what is the choice?
quiz.a: Test 3, occlusion and anchoring. The app needs a depth map of the real sofa, so the choice is MR; plain AR would draw the virtual sofa over the real one.

quiz.q: A headset shows the room through its cameras, tracks surfaces with depth sensors, and draws a virtual lamp that disappears behind the real sofa when the user walks past. Classify the system by all three tests and justify the label.
quiz.a: Test 1: the real room reaches the eye through camera pass-through, so it is not VR. Test 2: it registers virtual content to real surfaces using depth sensors, satisfying the AR requirement. Test 3: the lamp is occluded by the real sofa, which plain AR does not do. MR is AR plus depth sensing with anchoring and occlusion, so this is MR, specifically camera pass-through MR.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pass-through on consumer headsets blurs the line: the same device is VR with the cameras off and MR with them on and depth reconstruction running. Research is pushing dense depth out of a single moving camera, so occlusion stops needing a dedicated depth sensor. Search for passthrough MR, depth API occlusion, WebXR hit test and spatial anchors.
